accuracy.evidence: Checked 611 against NC Year 4 (describe the simple functions of the basic parts of the digestive system in humans) and the NHS/Britannica descriptions: order mouth-oesophagus-stomach-small intestine-large intestine-rectum/anus; peristalsis (not gravity) moves food, so swallowing works upside down and in orbit; stomach acid plus churning; nutrients and most water absorbed in the small intestine, with fats entering lymph first (stated in the adult text); large intestine reabsorbs remaining water; fibre is not absorbed. Transit hours in items stay inside typical ranges (stomach 2-4 h, small intestine 2-6 h).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented KS2 misconceptions: food falls straight from mouth to stomach or is moved by gravity (upside-down squeeze test), oesophagus confused with the windpipe (challenge distractor and m6), the stomach as the place nutrients are absorbed (prediction and challenge), small vs large intestine order and jobs, and fibre being absorbed (sort feedback).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaggut is built around the gut's own mechanisms: a labelled body map, chewing that doubles pieces, a muscle ring that pushes a bolus along the tube (with a flip to defeat the gravity idea), churning to a soup meter, and a wall-to-blood sort. flagnutri (diet), flagchain (food chains) and flagheart (circulation) share none of it; lab gate shingle overlap under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the learner perform the organ's job before the text names it: grinding to 16 wet pieces, pushing the food only by moving the muscle squeeze behind it (it works the same upside down), churning until the chunks dissolve, and deciding what crosses the intestine wall. The tour then links every part to its job.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: 'straight into the stomach' (label step shows the oesophagus tube), 'gravity pulls food down' (upside-down squeeze still works), 'soaks most of it into the blood' for the stomach (churn step), and 'the stomach' for where goodness enters the blood (sort step).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with a specific message for every wrong option: windpipe ('carries air to your lungs'), stomach ('churns, little goodness passes into the blood there'), large intestine ('mostly takes back water'), small intestine in the wrong position or job, mouth vs churning, and teeth vs oesophagus/small intestine jobs. Label and sort drops have their own slip messages too.

readability.evidence: Kid text FK grade 2.5, adult 9.5 (family targets 5.0 and 10.0). Short sentences, concrete words (bag, tube, soup) alongside the Year 4 terms oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, saliva, absorb, faeces, anus.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate clean. Each kid paragraph covers one stage of the trip with its job; adult paragraphs give the standard, the mechanisms (peristalsis, acid, absorption, lymph for fats), four named mistakes and what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on iPhone 13 (dark) and 360 px Android (light) for all 7 steps: body map labels sit clear of the torso, label/sort cards wrap to two rows, the squeeze tube and stomach fit with the message below, bins show their sorted items; young-size buttons below the canvas, nothing clipped.

accessibility.evidence: Button twins for every canvas action (pick a label then Part 1-5, Chew, Squeeze, Turn upside down, Churn, pick a card then a box, Follow a meal and one button per organ); the canvas aria-label is updated with every message; walk.cjs axe clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: Department for Education, National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, Year 4 Animals, including humans ('describe the simple functions of the basic parts of the digestive system in humans')

NHS and Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'human digestive system': peristalsis in the oesophagus, stomach acid and churning, absorption of nutrients in the small intestine (fats via lacteals and lymph), water reabsorption in the large intestine
